name: Medicine and Human Body
description: Questions covering: Anatomy and physiology, History of medicine, Diseases and immunology...

questions.question: Which organ in the human body is the largest internal organ and is responsible for detoxifying the organism?
questions.explanation_correct: The liver is the largest internal organ in humans, performing metabolic, filtration, and storage functions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The skin is the largest organ overall (but external), the lungs are responsible for gas exchange, and the large intestine absorbs water.

questions.question: Which bone is the longest and strongest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation_correct: The femur (thigh bone) carries most of the body weight and is able to withstand enormous mechanical loads.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The tibia is shorter, the humerus is in the arm, and the pelvic bone is a flat bone.

questions.question: Where in the human body are the three smallest bones located: the malleus, incus, and stapes?
questions.explanation_correct: The auditory ossicles amplify and transmit sound wave vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the inner ear.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The nose contains cartilage and nasal bones, and the bones in the foot and hand are significantly larger.

questions.question: What is the name of the main artery that carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle of the heart to the rest of the body?
questions.explanation_correct: The aorta (main artery) is the largest arterial vessel in the human body, with thick, elastic walls.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, the vena cava collects blood from the body to the heart, and the carotid artery supplies the head.

questions.question: Which blood cells are responsible for transporting oxygen and contain the red pigment hemoglobin?
questions.explanation_correct: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) have a biconcave disc shape and do not have a cell nucleus in their mature form.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Leukocytes are white blood cells (immunity), thrombocytes are blood platelets (clotting), and lymphocytes are a subtype of leukocytes.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest nerve in the human body, running from the lower back down each leg?
questions.explanation_correct: The sciatic nerve provides motor and sensory supply to the entire lower limb, and its compression causes painful sciatica.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The vagus nerve is the main nerve of the parasympathetic system, the trigeminal nerve is responsible for the face, and the radial nerve for the arm.

questions.question: Which valve in the heart prevents blood from flowing back from the left ventricle into the left atrium?
questions.explanation_correct: The mitral (bicuspid) valve regulates the flow of blood on the left, oxygenated side of the heart.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The tricuspid valve lies on the right side, and the aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves at the exit of the ventricles.

questions.question: What is the name of the fluid produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, which facilitates the digestion of fats?
questions.explanation_correct: Bile emulsifies fats in the duodenum, breaking them down into small droplets that are more easily processed by enzymes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pancreatic juice contains digestive enzymes, gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, and saliva contains amylase.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek physician from the island of Kos is called the 'father of medicine' and formulated a famous ethical oath for doctors?
questions.explanation_correct: Hippocrates rejected beliefs about the divine origin of diseases, looking for their causes in the patient's environment and diet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galen created the Roman medical system that lasted for centuries, Aesculapius is a mythical god, and Aristotle was a philosopher of nature.

questions.question: Which Scottish physician and microbiologist discovered penicillin in 1928, ushering in the era of antibiotics?
questions.explanation_correct: Fleming noticed that the mold Penicillium notatum inhibited the growth of staphylococcus bacteria on a contaminated Petri dish.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pasteur developed pasteurization and a rabies vaccine, Koch discovered the tuberculosis bacillus, and Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine.

questions.question: Which English physician in 1796 developed the world's first effective vaccine by inoculating a boy with cowpox virus?
questions.explanation_correct: Jenner noticed that milkmaids who contracted the mild cowpox became immune to the deadly smallpox.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pasteur developed vaccines in the 19th century, Salk created the polio vaccine in 1952, and Lister introduced antiseptics.

questions.question: Which French chemist proved that diseases are caused by microorganisms and developed the rabies vaccine?
questions.explanation_correct: Pasteur disproved the theory of spontaneous generation and revolutionized medicine and the food industry through the process of pasteurization.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Koch studied tuberculosis and anthrax bacteria, Ehrlich created salvarsan for syphilis, and Bernard described homeostasis.

questions.question: Which British surgeon in the 19th century introduced the principles of antisepsis in operating rooms, using carbolic acid to disinfect tools and wounds?
questions.explanation_correct: Lister's work drastically reduced the number of post-operative infections and gangrene, saving millions of patients.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Morton demonstrated ether anesthesia, Hunter was a pioneer of anatomy, and Semmelweis ordered doctors to wash hands before deliveries.

questions.question: Which Hungarian physician in the mid-19th century was the first to show that washing hands with a chlorine solution prevents deadly puerperal fever in women?
questions.explanation_correct: Semmelweis was rejected by the medical community of his time, and his contributions were recognized only after his death.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lister developed surgical antisepsis, Koch studied bacteria under a microscope, and Virchow was the creator of cellular pathology.

questions.question: What is the name of the proteins produced by B lymphocytes that recognize and neutralize pathogen antigens?
questions.explanation_correct: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) fit antigens like a key to a lock, marking them for phagocytes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Antigens are foreign molecules that trigger a reaction, interferons are antiviral proteins, and histamines trigger allergic reactions.

questions.question: Which deadly infectious disease, caused by the Variola virus, was completely eradicated worldwide in 1980?
questions.explanation_correct: Smallpox is the only human disease completely eradicated thanks to a global immunization program.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Plague still occurs rarely in rodents, polio exists only residually, and tuberculosis remains a dangerous bacterial disease.

questions.question: Which virus destroys the human immune system by attacking T CD4 helper lymphocytes, leading to AIDS?
questions.explanation_correct: HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus, which leads to the disease AIDS after years of infection.
questions.explanation_incorrect: HPV causes cervical cancer, HCV is the hepatitis C virus, and HSV is the herpes simplex virus.

questions.question: Which tropical disease is caused by the Plasmodium protozoan and transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes?
questions.explanation_correct: Malaria attacks the patient's erythrocytes, causing recurrent attacks of chills and high fever.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dengue and yellow fever are viral diseases, and African sleeping sickness is caused by a trypanosome transmitted by the tsetse fly.

questions.question: What is the name of the popular pain reliever and anti-inflammatory drug, acetylsalicylic acid, introduced at the end of the 19th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Aspirin was synthesized by Felix Hoffmann of the Bayer company, becoming one of the most widely used drugs in the world.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Paracetamol and ibuprofen were developed later and do not contain a salicylate group, and morphine is a strong opiate drug.

questions.question: Which hormone produced by pancreatic beta cells regulates blood glucose levels, and its deficiency leads to type 1 diabetes?
questions.explanation_correct: Insulin enables the transport of glucose from the blood into cells to generate energy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Glucagon acts oppositely by raising blood sugar, adrenaline is the fight-or-flight hormone, and cortisol is the stress hormone.

questions.question: Which three scientists discovered the double helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) in 1953?
questions.explanation_correct: James Watson and Francis Crick published the double helix model, relying on X-ray diffraction images taken by Rosalind Franklin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Fleming's team implemented penicillin, Darwin and Wallace described evolution, and Avery's team proved that DNA carries genetic information.

questions.question: How many pairs of homologous chromosomes does a healthy human have in most of their somatic cells?
questions.explanation_correct: The human genome contains a total of 46 chromosomes divided into 23 pairs, one pair of which are the sex chromosomes (XX or XY).
questions.explanation_incorrect: 46 is the total number of single chromosomes, 22 pairs are autosomes, and chimpanzees have 24 pairs.

questions.question: Which part of the brain is responsible for motor coordination, maintaining balance, and muscle tone?
questions.explanation_correct: The cerebellum lies in the posterior cranial fossa and integrates sensory information with motor commands from the cortex.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The cerebral cortex is responsible for thinking and memory, the medulla oblongata for vital functions (breathing), and the thalamus is a relay station.

questions.question: What is the name of the longest part of the human digestive system, where the actual absorption of nutrients takes place?
questions.explanation_correct: The small intestine has a length of about 5-6 meters in adults, and its absorptive surface is increased by millions of intestinal villi.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The large intestine is shorter and wider, the stomach mixes and pre-digests, and the esophagus only transports food.

questions.question: What is the name of the structure in the kidneys consisting of a glomerulus and a tubule, which is the basic functional unit of the kidney?
questions.explanation_correct: Each human kidney contains about a million nephrons that filter blood and produce primary urine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A neuron is a nerve cell, an alveolus is an air sac in the lungs, and an osteon is a structural unit of bone tissue.

questions.question: Which hormone, secreted by the adrenal medulla in stressful situations, accelerates the heart rate and prepares the body for fight or flight?
questions.explanation_correct: Adrenaline (epinephrine) acts instantly, causing dilation of pupils and bronchioles, and a release of glucose into the blood.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Thyroxine regulates metabolism, melatonin regulates sleep, and prolactin regulates lactation.

questions.question: Which Roman physician of the 2nd century AD performed numerous animal dissections and created an anatomical system that dominated Europe for 1500 years?
questions.explanation_correct: Claudius Galen wrote dozens of medical treatises. Since he relied on dissections of pigs and monkeys, his anatomy contained numerous errors repeated for centuries.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hippocrates lived in classical Greece, Vesalius refuted Galen's errors in the 16th century, and Celsus compiled an encyclopedia of Roman medicine.

questions.question: Which Flemish anatomist published the work 'De humani corporis fabrica' in 1543, revolutionizing anatomy through the dissection of human corpses?
questions.explanation_correct: Vesalius demonstrated over 200 errors in Galen's writings, which became the foundation of modern scientific anatomy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Harvey described blood circulation in the 17th century, Paré was an outstanding field surgeon, and Falloppio described the fallopian tubes.

questions.question: Which English physician in 1628 was the first to describe a complete system of blood circulation in the human body with the heart as a pump?
questions.explanation_correct: Harvey described systemic and pulmonary circulation in his work, refuting Galen's theory of a supposed tidal flow of blood in vessels.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Willis studied brain anatomy, Hooke studied plant cells, and Vesalius studied bones and muscles.

questions.question: What is the name of the body's defensive reaction to infection or injury, characterized by redness, swelling, pain, and elevated temperature?
questions.explanation_correct: Inflammation is a controlled influx of immune cells to damaged tissue to eliminate threats and initiate repair.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction, autoimmunity is the destruction of own tissues, and apoptosis is programmed cell death.

questions.question: Which organ of the lymphatic system is responsible for the selection and maturation of T lymphocytes in childhood and shrinks after puberty?
questions.explanation_correct: The thymus produces hormones stimulating immune development and undergoes involution (fat replacement) in adults.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The spleen destroys old erythrocytes, the tonsils protect the throat, and the thyroid regulates iodine metabolism.

questions.question: Which chemical substance, a precursor to dopamine, is used as the primary drug in the therapy of Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation_correct: L-DOPA crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted into the missing dopamine in the brain, relieving tremors.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Serotonin does not cross the blood-brain barrier when taken orally, haloperidol is a neuroleptic, and diazepam is a sedative.

questions.question: Which monk from Brno formulated the basic laws of inheritance of traits by crossing pea plants in the 19th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Mendel's laws describe the dominance and segregation of alleles, giving rise to modern classical genetics.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Darwin described natural selection, Morgan studied chromosomes in fruit flies, and de Vries studied mutations.

questions.question: What is the name of the liquid part of blood, constituting about 55% of its volume, composed mainly of water, proteins, and mineral salts?
questions.explanation_correct: Blood plasma transports nutrients, hormones, and carbon dioxide in the form of bicarbonate ions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Serum is plasma deprived of fibrinogen (clotting factor), lymph circulates in the lymphatic system, and cerebrospinal fluid protects the nervous system.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest muscle in the human body in terms of mass and volume, which extends the hip joint?
questions.explanation_correct: The gluteus maximus is responsible for maintaining an erect posture while walking.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The quadriceps femoris is the strongest functionally, the latissimus dorsi has the largest surface area, and the gastrocnemius flexes the foot.

questions.question: What is the name of the microscopic extensions of a neuron that receive nerve impulses from other cells and transmit them to the cell body?
questions.explanation_correct: Dendrites form branched dendritic trees that receive chemical and electrical signals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An axon is a single long extension that sends impulses, a synapse is a junction between cells, and myelin is a fatty sheath.

questions.question: Which long extension of a neuron conducting impulses away from the cell body to other cells is covered with a myelin sheath?
questions.explanation_correct: Axons in humans can reach lengths of over a meter (e.g., in the sciatic nerve) and transmit signals over long distances.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A dendrite receives signals, glia are supporting cells of the brain, and a neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger.

questions.question: Which endocrine gland lies at the base of the brain in the so-called sella turcica and controls the function of other glands?
questions.explanation_correct: The pituitary gland produces tropic hormones that stimulate the thyroid, adrenal glands, and gonads.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The pineal gland produces melatonin which regulates sleep cycles, the thyroid lies in the neck, and the adrenals lie above the kidneys.

questions.question: Which Polish surgeon was the first in the world to successfully resect a stomach due to cancer in 1881, laying the foundations of modern gastroenterology?
questions.explanation_correct: Ludwik Rydygier performed this breakthrough surgery in Chełmno. A year earlier, he performed the world's first stomach resection due to a peptic ulcer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mikulicz was his student and introduced surgical masks, Czerwiakowski was a surgical pioneer from the 18th century, and Chałubiński treated tuberculosis in Zakopane.

questions.question: Which Polish ophthalmologist invented the cryoapplicator in 1961 - a device for the cryotherapy of cataracts and retinal detachment?
questions.explanation_correct: Krwawicz's cryosurgical method involved freezing the lens to make it easier to extract, revolutionizing global ophthalmology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Wicherkiewicz studied glaucoma in the 19th century, Korczak was a pediatrician and educator, and Bierkowski was an ether pioneer in Poland.

questions.question: Which Polish immunologist and microbiologist discovered blood groups in 1926 and described the mechanism of serological conflict?
questions.explanation_correct: Hirszfeld introduced the A, B, O, and AB blood group designations adopted worldwide in 1928.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Weigl created the first vaccine for epidemic typhus, Bujwid established rabies vaccination stations, and Cybulski discovered adrenaline.

questions.question: Which Polish biologist and zoologist developed the first effective vaccine against epidemic typhus by breeding lice in his institute in Lviv?
questions.explanation_correct: Weigl's vaccine saved hundreds of thousands of lives during World War II, and its production provided shelter to Polish intellectuals acting as lice feeders.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hirszfeld studied blood groups, Cybulski studied adrenaline, and Banach was an outstanding Lviv mathematician.

questions.question: Which Polish physiologist was the first to isolate adrenaline—the hormone of the adrenal medulla—in 1895?
questions.explanation_correct: Cybulski, together with Adolf Beck, also described EEG waves in the brain and studied the physiology of the circulatory system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bujwid was a microbiology pioneer, Hirszfeld an immunology pioneer, and Biegański was a prominent internist and medical philosopher.

questions.question: Which white blood cells of the immune system mature in the thymus and are responsible for cell-mediated immunity?
questions.explanation_correct: T lymphocytes recognize infected host cells and assist other immune cells in destroying pathogens.
questions.explanation_incorrect: B lymphocytes produce antibodies, granulocytes fight bacteria and parasites, and macrophages engulf cell debris.

questions.question: Which white blood cells of the immune system are responsible for producing antibodies in response to antigens?
questions.explanation_correct: B lymphocytes transform into plasma cells secreting millions of antibody molecules after contacting an antigen.
questions.explanation_incorrect: T lymphocytes are helper or killer cells, monocytes are macrophage precursors, and eosinophils fight parasites.

questions.question: What is the name of the hypersensitivity reaction of the immune system to commonly harmless substances, such as pollen or peanuts?
questions.explanation_correct: An allergy is caused by excessive activation of IgE class immunoglobulins and mast cells releasing histamine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Autoimmunization is an attack on one's own tissues, immunotolerance is the lack of reaction to an antigen, and anemia is red blood cell deficiency.

questions.question: Which class of drugs, to which penicillin and amoxicillin belong, acts bactericidally by blocking the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall?
questions.explanation_correct: These antibiotics possess a characteristic beta-lactam ring that is targeted by bacterial enzymes (beta-lactamases).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Macrolides and tetracyclines block protein synthesis on ribosomes, and aminoglycosides disrupt translation.

questions.question: Which popular drug with pain-relieving and fever-reducing actions does not exhibit anti-inflammatory effects, and its overdose carries a risk of liver necrosis?
questions.explanation_correct: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) acts mainly in the central nervous system and is safe for the stomach, but toxic to the liver in large doses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ibuprofen, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), and naproxen are NSAIDs with strong anti-inflammatory actions.

questions.question: What is the name of the basic molecule building DNA and RNA, consisting of a sugar, a nitrogenous base, and a phosphate group?
questions.explanation_correct: Nucleotides link into long chains via phosphodiester bonds forming the backbone of the nucleic acid.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A nucleoside does not have a phosphate group, a codon is a triplet of nucleotides, and an amino acid builds proteins.

questions.question: Which nitrogenous base occurs in RNA molecules instead of the thymine present in DNA molecules?
questions.explanation_correct: Uracil pairs with adenine in RNA molecules using two hydrogen bonds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Adenine, cytosine, and guanine occur in both DNA and RNA.

questions.question: Which element of the human eye is responsible for accommodation, changing its shape to focus light on the retina?
questions.explanation_correct: The lens is suspended on ligaments connected to the ciliary body, which regulates its curvature.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The cornea is the tough, transparent outer layer of the eye, the iris regulates light entry through the pupil, and the vitreous body fills the inside of the eye.

questions.question: What is the name of the photoreceptors of the retina responsible for black-and-white vision, shapes, and motion in low light?
questions.explanation_correct: Rods are extremely sensitive to light but do not distinguish colors; there are about 120 million of them in the human eye.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cones are responsible for color vision and acuity in good light, ganglion cells send signals to the optic nerve, and the macula is a cluster of cones.

questions.question: What is the name of the photoreceptors of the retina responsible for color vision and high visual acuity in bright light?
questions.explanation_correct: Cones in the human eye are divided into three types, each responding to a different wavelength of light: blue, green, and red.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rods are responsible for vision in the dark, amacrine cells process signals, and the sclera is the outer protective coat of the eye.

questions.question: Which thyroid hormone contains four iodine atoms and regulates the metabolic rate throughout the body?
questions.explanation_correct: Thyroxine (T4) is the main hormone secreted by the thyroid gland, containing four iodine atoms, and is converted in tissues to the more active T3.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Triiodothyronine (T3) has three iodine atoms; calcitonin regulates calcium levels; reverse T3 is an inactive metabolite.

questions.question: What is the name of the four small glands lying on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, which regulate calcium-phosphate balance?
questions.explanation_correct: The parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises calcium levels in the blood by releasing it from bones.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Adrenal glands lie above the kidneys, salivary glands are in the oral cavity, and the thymus is in the mediastinum.

questions.question: Which part of the brainstem controls the body's basic vital functions, such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure?
questions.explanation_correct: The medulla oblongata contains autonomic centers, and its damage results in immediate death due to respiratory arrest.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The cerebellum is responsible for movements, the midbrain for visual and auditory reflexes, and the pons connects the cerebellum to the brain.

questions.question: What is the name of the thick bundle of nerve fibers connecting the right and left hemispheres of the brain, enabling the exchange of information between them?
questions.explanation_correct: The corpus callosum consists of over 200 million axons and facilitates the integration of hemispheric functions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The anterior commissure is a smaller lower bundle, the thalamus filters senses, and the hippocampus is responsible for memory.

questions.question: Which structure of the limbic system, shaped like a seahorse, is responsible for the consolidation of short-term memory into long-term memory?
questions.explanation_correct: Damage to the hippocampus prevents the memorization of new facts (anterograde amnesia), while preserving older memories.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The amygdala controls emotions (especially fear), the cingulate gyrus controls motivation, and the hypothalamus controls homeostasis.

questions.question: What is the name of the almond-shaped structure in the brain, responsible for processing emotions, especially fear and aggression?
questions.explanation_correct: The amygdala triggers stress and fear responses, playing a key role in emotional learning.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The hippocampus is responsible for memory, the thalamus is a relay station, and the pineal gland secretes melatonin.

questions.question: What is the name of the blood vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle itself, and their blockage causes a heart attack?
questions.explanation_correct: The coronary arteries (right and left) branch off directly from the aorta right at its exit from the heart.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pulmonary arteries carry blood to the lungs, carotid arteries to the brain, and venae cavae return blood from the body.

questions.question: Which part of the inner ear, resembling a snail shell, contains the actual organ of hearing (organ of Corti)?
questions.explanation_correct: The cochlea is filled with fluid, the vibrations of which stimulate the hair cells of the auditory organ to generate nerve impulses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Semicircular canals and the vestibule are responsible for the sense of balance, and the Eustachian tube equalizes pressure in the middle ear.

questions.question: Which structures in the inner ear, arranged in three perpendicular planes, are responsible for detecting head rotations?
questions.explanation_correct: The semicircular canals contain fluid (endolymph) and sensory cells registering angular acceleration.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The cochlea is used for hearing, and the ossicles and tympanic membrane amplify vibrations in the middle ear.

questions.question: Which Polish cardiac surgeon performed the first successful heart transplant in Poland in 1985 in Zabrze?
questions.explanation_correct: Professor Zbigniew Religa performed the operation on a patient in extreme heart failure, breaking ethical barriers in Polish medicine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zembala and Bochenek were Religa's assistants during this procedure, and Manteuffel was a pioneer of Polish thoracic surgery.

questions.question: Who performed the world's first human-to-human heart transplant in Cape Town in 1967?
questions.explanation_correct: Barnard transplanted a heart into 53-year-old Louis Washkansky, who survived 18 days after the surgery.
questions.explanation_incorrect: DeBakey was a pioneer of artificial ventricles, Kantrowitz performed the first transplant in an infant, and Shumway developed the surgical techniques used by Barnard.

questions.question: Which Polish physician and biochemist in 1911 isolated a substance from rice bran that prevented beri-beri and coined the term 'vitamin'?
questions.explanation_correct: Funk demonstrated the existence of amines essential for life (vita-amine), starting the science of vitamins.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cybulski studied hormones, Dietl reformed the Krynica health resort, and Rydygier was a surgeon.

questions.question: Which Polish physician and professor in the 19th century eradicated the plica polonica plague and popularized balneology in Krynica?
questions.explanation_correct: Dietl was the rector of the Jagiellonian University, proved the harmfulness of bloodletting, and created Polish balneoclimatology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Chalubinski discovered the Zakopane climate, Strus was a Renaissance court physician, and Oczko described mineral waters in the 16th century.

questions.question: Which court physician to Kings Sigismund Augustus and Stephen Bathory wrote an outstanding Renaissance work on pulse examination 'Sphygmicae artis' in the 16th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Jozef Strus (Struthius) was a professor in Padua and gained European fame as one of the outstanding experts on pulse and Renaissance cardiology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oczko wrote about syphilis and mineral waters, Petrycy translated Aristotle, and Maciej of Miechow wrote the first Polish medical book.

questions.question: What is the name of the immune reaction in which antibodies and lymphocytes attack the body's own healthy cells?
questions.explanation_correct: Autoimmune diseases (e.g., Hashimoto's, multiple sclerosis, lupus) result from a failure of tolerance to self-antigens.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Immunosuppression is the suppression of immunity with drugs, intolerance is a non-allergic enzyme deficiency (e.g., lactose), and allergy is hyperactivity to foreign pollen.

questions.question: Which organ is destroyed by the immune system in Hashimoto's disease, the most common cause of hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation_correct: Hashimoto's disease (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) leads to the slow destruction of this gland's parenchyma.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Destruction of the pancreas leads to diabetes, the adrenal glands to Addison's disease, and the liver is targeted in autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.question: Which cardiovascular disease is characterized by the deposition of lipid plaques in arterial walls, leading to their narrowing and stiffening?
questions.explanation_correct: Atherosclerosis is the main cause of ischemic heart disease and strokes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An aneurysm is a dilation of an arterial wall, varicose veins are a failure of venous valves, and thrombosis is the blockage of a vessel by a clot.

questions.question: What is the name of the dangerous, sudden drop in blood pressure caused by a systemic allergic reaction, threatening the patient's life?
questions.explanation_correct: Anaphylaxis requires immediate intramuscular administration of adrenaline, which constricts vessels and dilates bronchioles.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cardiogenic shock results from heart failure, neurogenic shock from nervous system damage, and thyroid storm is thyroid hormone poisoning.

questions.question: Which strong pain reliever from the opioid group, derived from opium, is the standard in managing cancer pain?
questions.explanation_correct: Morphine acts by strongly stimulating opioid receptors in the spinal cord and brain, suppressing pain transmission.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Codeine is a weaker opiate with cough-suppressant actions, tramadol is a synthetic opioid of medium potency, and fentanyl is a strong, short-acting synthetic.

questions.question: Which synthetic opioid is about 100 times stronger than morphine and is used in anesthesiology and as pain patches?
questions.explanation_correct: Fentanyl exhibits strong lipophilic action, allowing it to quickly penetrate the brain and work in minimal doses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Methadone treats heroin addiction, buprenorphine is a partial agonist, and oxycodone is an oral drug.

questions.question: What is the name of the class of drugs that lower blood cholesterol by blocking the HMG-CoA reductase enzyme in the liver?
questions.explanation_correct: Statins (e.g., atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) decrease LDL cholesterol production and stabilize atherosclerotic plaques.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Fibrates act mainly on triglycerides, beta-blockers slow the heart rate, and ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure.

questions.question: Which heart drugs block beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing the heart rate and lowering blood pressure?
questions.explanation_correct: Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, bisoprolol) protect the heart from the excessive influence of adrenaline.
questions.explanation_incorrect: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin, diuretics are water pills, and calcium blockers dilate vessels.

questions.question: What is the name of the process of synthesizing an RNA molecule on a DNA template, occurring in the cell nucleus?
questions.explanation_correct: Transcription is carried out by RNA polymerase, copying the gene sequence onto an mRNA strand.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Translation is protein synthesis on a ribosome, replication is DNA duplication, and reverse transcription is DNA synthesis on an RNA template.

questions.question: What is the name of the process of synthesizing a polypeptide chain (protein) on an mRNA template, occurring in the cytoplasm on ribosomes?
questions.explanation_correct: During translation, tRNA molecules deliver corresponding amino acids in accordance with codons on the mRNA strand.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Transcription creates RNA, replication copies DNA, and splicing is the removal of introns from pre-mRNA.

questions.question: What is the name of the process of removing non-coding sequences (introns) and joining coding sequences (exons) during pre-mRNA maturation?
questions.explanation_correct: Splicing (gene splicing) is carried out by the spliceosome complex in the cell nucleus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Translation is protein synthesis, mutation is a change in DNA, and polyadenylation is the addition of a poly-A tail to RNA.

questions.question: Which sex-linked genetic disorder involves impaired blood clotting due to the lack of factor VIII or IX?
questions.explanation_correct: Hemophilia affects almost exclusively males because the genes encoding clotting factors lie on the X chromosome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Color blindness is the inability to distinguish colors, cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, and an aneurysm is a vascular disorder.

questions.question: Which autosomal genetic disorder manifests as the production of excessively sticky mucus that damages the lungs and pancreas?
questions.explanation_correct: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in the gene for the CFTR channel protein.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hemophilia is a bleeding disorder, Huntington's is a dominant neurodegenerative disease, and Down syndrome is trisomy 21.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest joint in the human body, connecting the femur to the tibia?
questions.explanation_correct: The knee joint is a modified hinge joint, protected in front by a sesamoid bone - the patella.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The hip and shoulder joints are ball-and-socket joints, and the ankle joint is smaller.

questions.question: What is the name of the flat bone lying in the front of the chest, to which the ribs connect?
questions.explanation_correct: The sternum (breastbone) closes the rib cage in front and consists of the manubrium, body, and xiphoid process.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The clavicle connects the sternum to the scapula, the scapula lies in the back, and false ribs connect to the sternum indirectly.

questions.question: What is the name of the fluid filling the brain ventricles and the spinal cord canal, absorbing shocks?
questions.explanation_correct: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates in the subarachnoid space and is produced by the choroid plexuses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lymph circulates in the lymphatic system, plasma is a component of blood, and interstitial fluid bathes body cells.

questions.question: Which part of the eye focuses the most light entering the eye and is non-vascular, drawing oxygen from the air?
questions.explanation_correct: The cornea has greater optical power than the lens and must be perfectly transparent, so it does not contain blood vessels.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The lens is responsible for accommodation, the retina contains photoreceptors, and the choroid is a highly vascularized middle layer.

questions.question: What are the smallest blood vessels, where gas and nutrient exchange takes place between blood and tissues?
questions.explanation_correct: Capillaries have a wall built of a single layer of endothelial cells facilitating diffusion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arterioles and venules are larger supplying and draining vessels, and lymphatic vessels transport lymph.

questions.question: Which organ in the human body filters blood, removes excess water and urea, and regulates blood pressure?
questions.explanation_correct: The kidneys secrete the hormone erythropoietin (stimulating blood production) and renin affecting blood pressure.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The liver neutralizes toxins, the spleen filters old erythrocytes, and the bladder stores urine.

questions.question: Which hormone produced by the kidneys stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells (erythrocytes)?
questions.explanation_correct: Erythropoietin (EPO) is synthesized in the kidneys in response to tissue hypoxia; it is sometimes used as a doping agent.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Renin regulates pressure, adrenaline is a stress hormone, and aldosterone regulates sodium absorption.

questions.question: What is the name of the connective tissue connecting muscle to bone, built of strong collagen fibers?
questions.explanation_correct: A tendon transmits the force of muscle contraction to the bone, enabling joint movement.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A ligament connects bone to bone in a joint, cartilage cushions, and the capsule protects the joint.

questions.question: What is the name of the strong band of connective tissue that connects a bone to another bone, stabilizing joints?
questions.explanation_correct: Ligaments limit excessive joint mobility, and their sprain is a common sports injury.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A tendon connects muscle to bone, fascia surrounds muscles, and periosteum covers bones.

questions.question: What are the bone tissue cells responsible for building and mineralizing new bone called?
questions.explanation_correct: Osteoblasts (bone-forming cells) synthesize collagen and stimulate the deposition of calcium salts.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Osteoclasts are bone-resorbing cells that destroy bone, osteocytes are mature cells trapped in the matrix, and chondrocytes build cartilage.

questions.question: What are the bone tissue cells responsible for the destruction and resorption of old bone tissue called?
questions.explanation_correct: Osteoclasts (bone-resorbing cells) secrete acid and enzymes that dissolve bone minerals during skeleton remodeling.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Osteoblasts form bone, osteocytes are permanent cells, and chondroblasts form cartilage.

questions.question: Which tooth in the permanent human dentition has the longest root and is used for tearing food?
questions.explanation_correct: Canines have a cone-shaped crown and a single, very long and thick root firmly embedded in the alveolus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Incisors are used for biting off, and premolars and molars are for crushing and grinding food.

questions.question: How many permanent teeth does an adult human have, including the four wisdom teeth (third molars)?
questions.explanation_correct: The complete permanent dentition consists of 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, and 12 molars.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Deciduous dentition has 20 teeth, and an adult has 28 teeth after removing all wisdom teeth.

questions.question: What is the hardest tissue in the human body, covering the crown of the tooth and protecting it?
questions.explanation_correct: Enamel consists of 96% inorganic compounds, mainly hydroxyapatite crystals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dentin lies under the enamel, cementum covers the tooth root, and pulp is the vascularized living tissue inside.

questions.question: What is the name of the tissue lying under the enamel, building most of the tooth mass, and sensitive to pain?
questions.explanation_correct: Dentin has a yellowish color and is porous, containing dentinal tubules with cell extensions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Enamel protects the crown, pulp fills the chamber, and cementum covers the root.

questions.question: What is the name of the only living, highly vascularized and innervated tissue of the tooth, filling its chamber and canals?
questions.explanation_correct: Pulp nourishes the tooth from within; its inflammation requires root canal (endodontic) treatment.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dentin and enamel are hard tissues, and periosteum covers jaw bones.

questions.question: Which Polish internist and philosopher from Czestochowa wrote the influential textbook 'Medical Diagnostics' at the beginning of the 20th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Bieganski created outstanding works in the field of logic and medical ethics, referred to as the 'faultless physician'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Chalubinski studied the climate of Zakopane, Dietl balneology in Krakow, and Flatau was a well-known Warsaw neurologist.

questions.question: Which Polish neurologist described the neck reflex (Flatau's sign) in 1912 and wrote the first Polish monograph on migraine?
questions.explanation_correct: Flatau was a co-founder of Polish neurology and the author of a brain atlas recognized throughout Europe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Babinski described the famous plantar reflex in Paris, Orzechowski studied muscle tone, and Goldflam studied myasthenia.

questions.question: Which French-Polish neurologist described the plantar reflex in 1896, involving the dorsiflexion of the big toe, indicating pyramidal tract damage?
questions.explanation_correct: The Babinski sign is one of the most important and widely examined reflexes in clinical neurology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Flatau described the neck reflex, Goldflam studied myasthenia, and Funk discovered vitamins.

questions.question: Which infectious disease, known as the 'white plague', is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacillus discovered by Robert Koch?
questions.explanation_correct: Tuberculosis most often attacks the lungs, and its bacilli are protected by a thick, waxy lipid envelope making treatment difficult.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, cholera by Vibrio cholerae, and leprosy by Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.question: Which infectious disease, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, decimated Europe in the 14th century under the name 'Black Death'?
questions.explanation_correct: Plague is transmitted to humans by fleas parasitizing rats; it occurs in bubonic or pneumonic forms.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cholera spreads through contaminated water, typhus through body lice, and chickenpox is a viral disease.

questions.question: What is the name of the parasitic disease caused by pinworms, very common in preschool children?
questions.explanation_correct: Enterobiasis (pinworm infection) spreads easily through direct contact and inhalation due to parasite eggs in dust.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ascariasis is an infection with roundworms, taeniasis with tapeworms, and toxoplasmosis with a protozoan from cats.

questions.question: Which group of drugs, to which diazepam and alprazolam belong, acts as anxiolytics by enhancing the action of the neurotransmitter GABA?
questions.explanation_correct: Benzodiazepines exhibit strong sedative, anxiolytic, and sleep-inducing actions, but their long-term use leads to addiction.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Barbiturates are older, more toxic sleep aids, neuroleptics treat psychoses, and TCAs are antidepressants.

questions.question: Which inhibitory neurotransmitter is the primary target of action for benzodiazepines and sleep aids in the brain?
questions.explanation_correct: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) inhibits neuronal excitability, producing a calming and muscle-relaxing effect.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter, noradrenaline excites attention, and acetylcholine regulates muscle contractions.

questions.question: What are angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors commonly used for in the treatment of arterial hypertension?
questions.explanation_correct: ACE inhibitors (e.g., ramipril, enalapril) block the formation of angiotensin II - a hormone that constricts blood vessels.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Beta-blockers slow the heart, sartans block the angiotensin receptor, and statins lower cholesterol.
